title: SQL Server Statements Explained
intro: A practical guide to reading and writing common SQL Server statements with confidence.

sections.title: 1. SELECT: read the data you need
sections.body: SELECT chooses columns and reads rows from one or more tables. Start with explicit column names instead of SELECT * so the query stays stable when the table changes.
sections.example:
SELECT CustomerId, FullName, Email
FROM dbo.Customers;
sections.sample:
CustomerId | FullName       | Email
101        | Asha Patel    | asha@example.com
102        | Daniel Wong   | daniel@example.com
sections.output:
CustomerId | FullName       | Email
101        | Asha Patel    | asha@example.com
102        | Daniel Wong   | daniel@example.com
sections.note: The FROM clause identifies the source table. The result contains only the three requested columns.
sections.scenario: A customer profile screen can use this query to load the fields it needs without transferring private or unused columns.

sections.title: 2. WHERE: filter rows early
sections.body: WHERE applies conditions before rows are returned. Use parameters from application code and compare dates with ranges when you need reliable index usage.
sections.example:
SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, TotalAmount
FROM dbo.Orders
WHERE Status = @Status
  AND CreatedAt >= @StartDate
  AND CreatedAt < @EndDate;
sections.sample:
OrderId | CustomerId | Status    | CreatedAt           | TotalAmount
5001    | 101        | Completed | 2026-09-20 09:15:00 | 125.00
5002    | 101        | Pending   | 2026-09-20 10:30:00 | 80.00
sections.note: @Status, @StartDate and @EndDate should be parameters, not string-concatenated values.
sections.scenario: An admin report can safely fetch only completed orders for one business day while avoiding SQL injection and accidental time-zone boundaries.

sections.title: 3. JOIN: combine related data
sections.body: JOIN connects rows through related keys. INNER JOIN returns matching rows only; LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table even when a related row does not exist. RIGHT JOIN keeps every row from the right table, although many teams prefer rewriting it as a LEFT JOIN for readability.
sections.example:
-- Matching orders only
SELECT o.OrderId, c.FullName
FROM dbo.Orders AS o
INNER JOIN dbo.Customers AS c ON c.CustomerId = o.CustomerId;

-- Keep customers with no orders
SELECT c.CustomerId, c.FullName, o.OrderId
FROM dbo.Orders AS o
RIGHT JOIN dbo.Customers AS c ON c.CustomerId = o.CustomerId;

-- Equivalent, usually clearer LEFT JOIN
SELECT c.CustomerId, c.FullName, o.OrderId
FROM dbo.Customers AS c
LEFT JOIN dbo.Orders AS o ON o.CustomerId = c.CustomerId;
sections.sample:
Customers: CustomerId | FullName
101        | Asha Patel
102        | Daniel Wong

Orders: OrderId | CustomerId | TotalAmount
5001    | 101        | 125.00
sections.output:
INNER JOIN: 5001 | Asha Patel
RIGHT/LEFT JOIN: 5001 | Asha Patel
                NULL | Daniel Wong
sections.note: Put the relationship in ON. Keep business filters in WHERE so the query is easier to reason about.
sections.scenario: An order list can show the customer name without duplicating customer data in the Orders table.

sections.title: 4. LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN: preserve unmatched rows
sections.body: Use LEFT JOIN when every row from the first table must remain in the result. Use RIGHT JOIN when every row from the second table must remain; in practice, swapping table order and using LEFT JOIN is often easier to read.
sections.example:
SELECT c.FullName, o.OrderId
FROM dbo.Customers AS c
LEFT JOIN dbo.Orders AS o
  ON o.CustomerId = c.CustomerId
ORDER BY c.FullName;

SELECT c.FullName, o.OrderId
FROM dbo.Orders AS o
RIGHT JOIN dbo.Customers AS c
  ON c.CustomerId = o.CustomerId;
sections.sample:
Customers: CustomerId | FullName
101        | Asha Patel
102        | Daniel Wong

Orders: OrderId | CustomerId
5001    | 101
sections.output:
FullName       | OrderId
Asha Patel     | 5001
Daniel Wong    | NULL
sections.note: A NULL OrderId means the customer exists but has no matching order. Be careful not to put a right-table filter in WHERE when you intend to preserve unmatched rows.
sections.scenario: A customer success report can list every customer, including new customers who have not placed an order yet.

sections.title: 5. OFFSET/FETCH: paginate ordered results
sections.body: OFFSET skips a number of rows and FETCH NEXT returns the next page. Always pair pagination with a deterministic ORDER BY, preferably including a unique tie-breaker.
sections.output:
Rows 41-60 in CreatedAt DESC, OrderId DESC order
For this 42-row sample: rows 41 and 42
sections.note: Large offsets can become slower because SQL Server still has to walk past skipped rows. For very large datasets, keyset pagination can be a better fit.
sections.scenario: An admin order grid can request page 3 with 20 rows per page while keeping navigation stable as long as the sort columns are deterministic.

sections.title: 6. GROUP BY: summarize rows
sections.body: GROUP BY creates one result row per group. Every selected column must either be grouped or wrapped in an aggregate such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN or MAX.
sections.example:
SELECT CustomerId, COUNT(*) AS OrderCount,
       SUM(TotalAmount) AS LifetimeValue
FROM dbo.Orders
GROUP BY CustomerId;
sections.note: The query produces one summary row per customer rather than returning each individual order.
sections.scenario: A CRM dashboard can rank customers by order count and total value without loading every order into the application.

sections.title: 5. HAVING: filter groups
sections.body: HAVING filters after GROUP BY has created groups. Use WHERE for row-level filters and HAVING for aggregate conditions.
sections.example:
SELECT CustomerId, SUM(TotalAmount) AS LifetimeValue
FROM dbo.Orders
WHERE Status = 'Completed'
GROUP BY CustomerId
HAVING SUM(TotalAmount) >= 10000;
sections.note: WHERE removes non-completed orders before grouping; HAVING keeps only high-value customer groups.
sections.scenario: A loyalty process can find customers eligible for a premium support tier based on completed purchase value.

sections.title: 6. ORDER BY: make result order explicit
sections.body: SQL tables do not have a guaranteed natural order. ORDER BY defines the order returned to the caller, and a unique tie-breaker makes paging predictable.
sections.note: The second sort column prevents rows with the same CreatedAt value from moving between pages.
sections.scenario: A support queue can consistently show the newest tickets first even when multiple tickets arrive in the same millisecond.

sections.title: 7. INSERT: add data deliberately
sections.body: INSERT creates rows. Name the target columns, validate input in the application and database, and capture the generated key when the next operation depends on it.
sections.sample:
Customers before insert: CustomerId | FullName | Email
101 | Daniel Wong | daniel@example.com
sections.note: A unique constraint on Email should enforce the business rule at the database boundary too.
sections.scenario: A registration endpoint can insert a customer and use the returned CustomerId to create the initial preferences row.

sections.title: 8. UPDATE: change only intended rows
sections.body: UPDATE is powerful because it can affect many rows. Always verify the WHERE clause with a SELECT first, and use a transaction when related changes must succeed together.
sections.example:
UPDATE dbo.Orders
SET Status = @NewStatus, UpdatedAt = SYSUTCDATETIME()
WHERE OrderId = @OrderId
  AND Status = 'Pending';
sections.note: The old status condition prevents a late worker from overwriting a newer state transition.
sections.scenario: A background payment worker can mark only still-pending orders as paid, making retries safer.

sections.title: 9. DELETE: remove with a safety check
sections.body: DELETE permanently removes rows unless the database is protected by a retention or soft-delete design. Preview the exact rows and use a transaction before destructive operations.
sections.note: In production, prefer a scheduled cleanup job with limits, monitoring and an established retention policy.
sections.scenario: An operations job can remove expired login sessions while recording how many rows were affected.

sections.title: 10. MERGE: use cautiously for synchronization
sections.body: MERGE can combine insert and update behavior, but its concurrency and edge cases make it harder to review. For critical systems, separate UPDATE and INSERT statements inside a transaction are often clearer.
sections.example:
MERGE dbo.ProductStock AS target
USING @StockChanges AS source
  ON target.ProductId = source.ProductId
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET Quantity = source.Quantity
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (ProductId, Quantity)
  VALUES (source.ProductId, source.Quantity);
sections.note: Test duplicate source keys, concurrent writes, constraints and error handling before adopting MERGE for production synchronization.
sections.scenario: A nightly import may synchronize inventory, but a stored procedure with explicit statements can be easier to retry and audit.

sections.title: 11. Transactions: keep a unit of work together
sections.body: A transaction groups changes so they commit together or roll back together. TRY...CATCH with XACT_STATE helps avoid leaving a transaction open after an error.
sections.note: Keep transactions short. Long transactions hold locks, increase blocking and make recovery harder.
sections.scenario: A money transfer must not debit one account unless the credit to the other account also succeeds.

sections.title: 12. Stored procedures: centralize database work
sections.body: Stored procedures can centralize validation, permissions and multi-step data operations. Use clear parameters, SET NOCOUNT ON and predictable result shapes.
sections.note: Treat procedure parameters and result sets as an API contract between the database and application.
sections.scenario: Several services can use the same audited order lookup without each service reimplementing the joins and filters.

sections.title: 13. Views: expose reusable read models
sections.body: A view stores a reusable SELECT definition. It can simplify reporting and hide join complexity, but it does not automatically solve performance problems or replace good indexes.
sections.example:
CREATE OR ALTER VIEW dbo.vw_OrderSummary
AS
SELECT o.OrderId, c.FullName, o.Status, o.TotalAmount
FROM dbo.Orders AS o
JOIN dbo.Customers AS c ON c.CustomerId = o.CustomerId;
sections.sample:
Orders: 5001 | CustomerId 101 | Completed | 125.00
Customers: 101 | Asha Patel
sections.output:
OrderId | FullName    | Status    | TotalAmount
5001    | Asha Patel  | Completed | 125.00
sections.note: Use views for stable read models and permissions boundaries; document the underlying tables and expected filters.
sections.scenario: A reporting team can query a consistent order summary while the application keeps normalized tables underneath.

sections.title: 14. Debugging patterns
sections.body: Debug from the data outward: reproduce with the smallest input, inspect the actual query and parameters, check row counts, review the execution plan, and look for blocking or constraint errors. SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON enables diagnostic messages for the next statements: IO reports data access and TIME reports CPU and elapsed duration. SET STATISTICS IO, TIME OFF turns those messages off again.
sections.output:
OrderId | TotalAmount
5001    | 125.00
5002    | 80.00

STATISTICS IO example:
Table 'Orders': logical reads 3, physical reads 0, read-ahead reads 0

STATISTICS TIME example:
CPU time = 2 ms, elapsed time = 4 ms
sections.note: Read logical reads as the pages SQL Server processed from memory, physical reads as pages fetched from disk, and read-ahead reads as pages prefetched. CPU time is processor work; elapsed time is total wall-clock duration and may include waits. Compare the same parameters before and after a change, and use SET STATISTICS only for diagnostics, not as a replacement for an actual execution plan. Useful checks also include sys.dm_exec_requests for active work and sys.dm_tran_locks for blocking.
sections.scenario: If an endpoint becomes slow, compare logical reads and duration before and after an index or query change, rather than guessing from application latency alone.
